headline: Shagwong to the Lighthouse: Blues Blitz While Bass Hold for the Moon
subhead: The bunker wall along the ocean beaches is drawing blitzing bluefish and staged bass, and the bonito are finally within reach from the east.
body_markdown:
Early September at the Point always feels like the top of a hill you can see over but haven't crested yet. The water off the Lighthouse is still holding in the upper 60s, bunker schools are thick and visible from the bluffs at Camp Hero down through the South side beaches, and everything about this week says the fall run is loaded and waiting on a trigger. That trigger is the moon. It's building toward full on the 6th and 7th, and with it comes stronger tidal push through the rips at North Bar and off the Lighthouse — the kind of current that takes a scattered, non-committal bunker school and squeezes it into something a big bass can't ignore. We're not there yet. But we're close enough that this is the week to start paying attention every single tide.

Here's the honest read on where things stand. Striped bass are around in real numbers, but they're staged on the bait rather than blitzing it. Water in the low-to-mid 70s along the beaches is still warm enough to keep them lazy and scattered during daylight, which means the best action right now is a dawn and dusk game, not a mid-day one. Boats working the boulder field off the Point on the building tide are picking at bass in the 20 to 34-inch range on bucktails and swimming plugs, with the occasional better fish mixed in for those willing to work the deeper edges off Turtle Cove on the last of the ebb. Surf guys working the South side rocks at first light on bunker spoons and Danny plugs are connecting, but it's a fish-here, fish-there bite, not a wall of rods bent.

Bluefish are the one thing that hasn't needed an excuse this week. They've been the most dependable bite on the whole East End, and Montauk's version of it has been legitimate — schools working bunker pods from the Lighthouse rip down through Shagwong Reef, with blitzes breaking on the surface hard enough to see gulls diving from the bluff road. Poppers and 2-ounce bunker spoons trolled or cast into the boils have been drawing quick, violent strikes, and these aren't dink blues — plenty of 6 to 10-pound fish mixed through the schools. If you want a guaranteed bend in the rod this week, this is it. Work the edges of the bait, not the thickest part of the ball, and keep moving with the school because these blitzes don't sit still.

Fluke are winding down the way they always do this time of year, and Montauk's version is no exception. The doormat-class fish that were holding in Fort Pond Bay and around the harbor structure through August have started sliding out toward deeper ocean-side rubble and rock piles, which is the classic pre-migration move. There's still a fish to be had on white Gulp Swimming Mullets and chartreuse bucktails worked slow along the drop-offs outside the harbor mouth, but the numbers are thinning fast and this bite has maybe another week or two of real relevance before it's mostly a memory until next spring. Porgies, on the other hand, remain a sure thing — Shagwong Reef and the rock piles off Frisbie's continue to give up steady catches on sandworms and clam bellies fished on the bottom, incoming water, and that's a bite that'll carry right through the fall with little drama.

We flagged this a week back — that the bait balls building along the beaches and a bonito push working in from the east would open this zone up to more variety, and that's exactly the shape things are taking. The bonito run out of Block Island and Point Judith has continued pushing west, and it's now within range of Block Island Sound and the Race, which puts Montauk in position to see them show in the next several days if the pattern holds. There's also squid building up in Rhode Island and Nantucket Sound water, and once that forage starts filtering into the Montauk rips, it tends to supercharge everything from bass to bonito to false albacore. None of that has fully arrived yet, but the ingredients are lining up the way they do right before this place turns into what it's famous for.

Looking at the next few days, the pattern to watch is the moon and the bait. If the bunker schools along the South side beaches and off the Point keep thickening while the tide strengthens toward the full moon, the odds of a real surface blitz — the kind where bass, blues, and maybe the first albies of the season all show at once — go up significantly by the weekend. Until that trigger fires, the smart play is working the bluefish blitzes for guaranteed action, hitting the boulder field and Turtle Cove on the early flood for bass, and treating the fluke bite as a bonus rather than a target. Keep an eye on Shagwong and the Lighthouse rip for the first real signs the variety is expanding — that's usually how it starts out here, one species at a time until the whole Point lights up with all of them at once.
